elements.quote: In this living systematic review and meta-analyses, we searched seven electronic databases for crosssectional studies and longitudinal studies on psychological problems on COVID-19 patients from Jan 1, 2020 to Oct 7, 2020.
elements.reason: The abstract explicitly calls the work a "living systematic review and meta-analyses," identifying the report as a systematic review.

elements.quote: Objectives: We aimed to investigate the psychological problems on people infected with SARS-CoV-2 during the pandemic.
elements.reason: The abstract provides a clear statement of the main objective/review question.

elements.quote: we searched seven electronic databases for crosssectional studies and longitudinal studies on psychological problems on COVID-19 patients from Jan 1, 2020 to Oct 7, 2020.
elements.reason: The abstract specifies study designs (cross-sectional and longitudinal) and population (COVID-19 patients) and date range, which serves as partial inclusion criteria, but it does not explicitly state detailed inclusion and exclusion criteria.

elements.quote: we searched seven electronic databases for crosssectional studies and longitudinal studies on psychological problems on COVID-19 patients from Jan 1, 2020 to Oct 7, 2020.
elements.reason: The abstract reports that seven electronic databases were searched and provides the date range (to Oct 7, 2020), but it does not name the specific information sources in the abstract.

elements.quote: and assessed the study quality based on the 11-item checklist recommended by the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality.
elements.reason: The abstract states the method used to assess study quality/risk of bias (the 11-item AHRQ checklist).

elements.quote: We pooled data for prevalence with their 95% confidence interval (CI) using random effect models
elements.reason: The abstract describes the synthesis method (meta-analysis pooling prevalence using random effects and reporting 95% CIs).

elements.quote: Fourty-four studies, including studies from China(35), Italy(2), Iran(2), India(1), Korea(1), Ecuador(1), Switzerland(1), Germany(1), were identified by comprising a total of 8587 completed questionnaires and 38 studies for meta-analyses.
elements.reason: The abstract reports the total number of included studies (44), number contributing to meta-analysis (38), total participants (8,587 completed questionnaires), and summarizes study locations/characteristics.

elements.quote: The prevalence of anxiety, depression, post-traumatic stress disorder(PTSD), insomnia, somatization, and fear in patients with COVID-19 was 16.6% (10.1%-23.1%), 37.7% (29.3%-46.2%), 41.5% (9.3%-73.7%), 68.3% (48.6%-88.0%), 36.5% (20.2%-52.8%), 47.6% (9.4%-85.7%), respectively.
elements.reason: The abstract presents results for the main outcomes, giving prevalence estimates and 95% CIs for each outcome.

elements.quote: We pooled data for prevalence with their 95% confidence interval (CI) using random effect models ... The prevalence of anxiety, depression ... was 16.6% (10.1%-23.1%), 37.7% (29.3%-46.2%) ...
elements.reason: A meta-analysis was conducted and the abstract reports summary estimates with 95% confidence intervals for outcomes.

elements.quote: The prevalence of anxiety, depression, and insomnia in severe COVID-19 patients (intensive care unit inpatients) was higher than mild or clinically stable COVID-19 patients.
elements.reason: The abstract compares groups and indicates the direction of effect (higher prevalence in severe patients).

elements.quote: Limitations: A significant degree of heterogeneity in terms of populations, sampling methods, scales was noted across studies.
elements.reason: The abstract briefly summarizes important limitations of the included evidence, citing heterogeneity in populations, sampling, and scales.

elements.quote: Conclusions: There existed high proportions of COVID-19 patients with psychological problem. The prevalence of psychological problems was closely related to the patients themselves, their surroundings and social support. It is imperative to provide ontime psychological care service for COVID-19 patients and to follow-up them for a longer period.
elements.reason: The abstract provides a general interpretation of results and discusses important implications and recommendations.
No funding source is reported in the abstract evidence provided.
The abstract does not provide a register name or registration number; no registration information is present in the supplied abstract evidence.

elements.quote: Limitations: A significant degree of heterogeneity in terms of populations, sampling methods, scales was noted across studies.
elements.reason: The abstract notes a key uncertainty/limitation (substantial heterogeneity across studies), but there is no broader description of the current state of knowledge (e.g. summary of prior literature or gaps) beyond reporting the review's objectives and findings, so the criterion is only partially met.

elements.quote: Objectives: We aimed to investigate the psychological problems on people infected with SARS-CoV-2 during the pandemic.
elements.reason: The abstract states the review objective and the conclusion emphasizes the need for timely psychological care and follow-up, explaining the importance and need for conducting the review.
No evidence was provided describing the relationship to existing similar systematic reviews, nor citing or explaining the need relative to prior reviews or updates.
The review addresses prevalence of psychological problems in COVID-19 patients (observational studies), not effects of interventions; thus describing an intervention mechanism is not applicable.
The review is not of complex interventions or delivery contexts; no interventions are evaluated, so a logic model is not applicable.

elements.quote: Objectives: We aimed to investigate the psychological problems on people infected with SARS-CoV-2 during the pandemic.
elements.reason: The review objective is explicitly stated, but it is not framed using a formal question‑formulation framework (e.g., PICO or equivalent).

elements.quote: In this living systematic review and meta-analyses, we searched seven electronic databases for crosssectional studies and longitudinal studies on psychological problems on COVID-19 patients from Jan 1, 2020 to Oct 7, 2020. The primary outcome was prevalence of various psychological problems such as anxiety, depression, stress, insomnia, somatization, and fear.
elements.reason: This review addresses prevalence in observational studies rather than intervention effects, so specifying planned comparisons using PICO is not applicable.

elements.quote: Population: people infected by SARS-CoV-2, regardless of age, gender, race, including suspected SARS-CoV-2 infected patients without a clear nucleic acid diagnosis but with highly suspected clinical performance; Research design: Observational studies, including cross-sectional studies (such as epidemiological survey, questionnaire survey, on­ line survey, etc) and longitudinal studies; Published or pre-print published articles, conference articles or other gray documents; Outcome indicators: prevalence of different psychological problems and associated factors, such as depression, anxiety, stress, insomnia, somatization, and fear.
elements.reason: The manuscript specifies population, eligible study designs, types of reports, and outcomes, but does not state follow-up requirements or other study characteristic details (e.g., minimum follow-up duration) required by the element.

elements.quote: The COVID-19 mental health database was established via the NoteExpress software (V3.3.0, Beijing Aiqinhai Lezhi Technology Co., Ltd.), which included the literature on mental health studies related to COVID-19 since January 1, 2020. ... The publication language included in the study was English or Chinese.
elements.reason: The review specifies the timeframe (since January 1, 2020) and languages (English or Chinese). Publication/report status (published or pre-print) is also specified elsewhere (text_7), demonstrating eligible report characteristics.
No explicit distinction is provided between excluding studies because outcomes were not measured versus excluding because outcome results were not reported.

elements.quote: Outcome indicators: prevalence of different psychological problems and associated factors, such as depression, anxiety, stress, insomnia, somatization, and fear.
elements.reason: The review specifies outcome groups (depression, anxiety, stress, etc.) used in synthesis, but does not link these groups to specific comparisons defined in the review objectives or describe how studies were grouped for each synthesis.
No rationale is provided for notable restrictions on study eligibility (e.g., reasons for language, date, or design restrictions are not explained).

elements.quote: The COVID-19 mental health database will update the search every six months. ... The latest version of the COVID-19 mental health database had been updated to 7 th October 2020.
elements.reason: A date for the database update is reported (7 October 2020) and the update frequency is given, but dates when each individual information source (each database/register/website) was last searched are not reported.

elements.quote: Based on the comprehensive search of seven electronic databases, including PubMed, Embase, PsycInfo, Wanfang Data, Chongqing VIP, Sinomed, and China National Knowledge Infrastructure (CNKI)... which included the literature on mental health studies related to COVID-19 since January 1, 2020.
elements.reason: Names of the bibliographic databases and a coverage start date (since January 1, 2020) are reported, but the search interface/platform for each database is not specified.

elements.reason: The types of individuals contacted (authors of original studies) and contact methods are explicitly described.

elements.reason: The manuscript explicitly states that the full search strategies for all electronic databases are provided in the supplementary file, indicating the complete search strategies are reported (in supplementary material).

elements.quote: The prevalence rate was defined as the number of cases detected divided by sample size and standard error. ... The inverse variance method of DerSimonian and Laird (adjustment) (DerSimonian and Laird, 2015) was adopted to calculate the prevalence rate and the integrated prevalence of estimates and 95% confidence interval (CI).
elements.reason: The manuscript explicitly defines the effect measure used for outcomes (prevalence rate) and states the method used to calculate pooled prevalence and 95% CIs (inverse variance DerSimonian and Laird).
No text in the provided evidence describes thresholds or ranges used to interpret effect size (e.g., categorizations or rationale for interpreting prevalence magnitudes).
No description was provided of methods to re-express synthesized results using another effect measure in the supplied evidence.

The manuscript does not provide a justification for the choice of effect measure beyond reporting that prevalence and 95% CIs were calculated; no rationale or justification is given in the provided evidence.

elements.quote:
The two authors (F Dong and HL Liu) independently selected liter­ ature and extracted data and cross-checked the repetition. If two or more papers came from the same research, the most complete paper with the most detailed reports were selected. Any disagreement would be settled through adjudication based on discussion or consultation with a third member of the research group. First, the titles and abstracts of the literature were read. Then the full texts were read to determine whether they could be included in the research. If the important information involved in the research was missing or unclear, we would contact the author of the original study through emails and telephone.

Thirty-eight studies were included in the meta-analyses, and inte­ grated analysis was made on the prevalence rates of abnormal psycho­ logical problems, such as anxiety, depression, PTSD, insomnia, somatization, and fear.

Through the preliminary screening of COVID-19 mental health database, 26,590 literature were selected. After the repetition was excluded, there were 15,503 left. After reviewing the titles and abstracts, we finally established the COVID-19 mental health database (dynamic version, Date 19/02/2021), including 5,185 papers. In this database, through browsing the titles and the abstracts, papers without obvious relations with the theme of this systematic review were excluded, then 77 articles were reviewed and classified, and 44 of them were finally included in this review.(see Fig. 1)
elements.reason: The manuscript describes general study selection and screening steps (title/abstract screening, full-text review, duplicate handling, arbitration) and reports that 38 studies were included in meta-analyses, but it does not describe the specific processes used to decide which studies were eligible for each synthesis (e.g., how studies were tabulated or compared against planned groups for each synthesis or criteria for including particular outcomes in each synthesis). Therefore the requirement is only partially met.

elements.quote: The prevalence rate was defined as the number of cases detected divided by sample size and standard error. To incorporate a study into the meta-analyses, two conditions have to be met: 1) it should determine the results using a recognized scale rather than self-designed questionnaires; 2) the number of result indicators or the scores of specific items in the scale should be accurately reported. The inverse variance method of DerSimonian and Laird (adjustment) (DerSimonian and Laird, 2015) was adopted to calculate the prevalence rate and the integrated prevalence of estimates and 95% confidence interval (CI). ... sensitivity analysis was conducted to test the abnormal values that may occur, excluding the research that failed to clearly report the investigation time or survey time point; ... Because of the heterogeneity of the studies on patients from different countries, we used the narrative analysis to summarize the outstanding findings of the studies included in the systematic review, and presented the results with tables.
elements.reason: The manuscript describes some methods used to prepare and include data for synthesis (definitions of prevalence, inclusion criteria for meta-analysis, use of DerSimonian and Laird inverse-variance method, use of sensitivity and subgroup analyses, and narrative summary). However, it does not explicitly describe procedures for handling missing summary statistics or specific data conversions (e.g., how missing variances or non-standard summary measures would be imputed or transformed), so the reporting is incomplete.

elements.quote: Data extraction table included: 1) first author, research subject, date of publication; 2) research characteristics: population category, country, research location, number of participants; 3) key factors of assessing bias and risks: response rate, research method, sampling method, survey scale, survey method, the number of effective questionnaires, survey time, survey node; 4) result indicators and result measurement data: the number of reports of anxiety, depression, stress disorder, insomnia, etc., and relevant grouping data and risk factors were also included.
elements.reason: The manuscript explicitly describes the structure and the data fields included in the data extraction table (i.e., what columns/data are in the tabular display).

elements.quote: the results of the meta-analyses were represented by forest plot. ... Meta-analyses were performed using Stata v16.0 (StataCorp LLC). Because of the heterogeneity of the studies on patients from different countries, we used the narrative analysis to summarize the outstanding findings of the studies included in the systematic review, and presented the results with tables. Fig. 1. Flow diagram of the selection of studies for the systematic review and meta-analyses.
elements.reason: The methods section states the graphical method used for meta-analysis results (forest plots) and references a flow diagram (Fig. 1); it also notes presentation with tables, indicating how results are visually/tabularly displayed.

elements.quote: We considered using the subgroup analysis for the different stages and degrees of patients with SARS-CoV-2 infection, and divided the patients into overall patients with no distinguishing feature, patients with mild symptoms or clinically stable patients, severe patients (...), discharged patients, patients with suspected infection based on their characteristics; ... according to the investigation time, the studies were divided into the first stage (from January to the beginning of February 2020), the second stage (from mid-February to mid-March 2020), the third stage (after late March 2020); or according to the time point of the investigation, the studies were divided into the studies during hospitalization or just completed the definite diagnosis, and the follow-up investigation conducted when or after the patients left the hospital.
elements.reason: The manuscript describes the basis for grouping studies (by patient severity/stage, investigation time periods, and timing relative to hospitalization), which indicates how studies would be ordered or grouped in analyses, tables or graphs.

No text in the provided evidence explains a rationale for using any non-standard graphs; only standard graphs (forest plot, flow diagram) and tables are mentioned without justification for non-standard visualizations.

elements.quote: Meta-analyses were performed using Stata v16.0 (StataCorp LLC).
elements.reason: The software and version used for statistical synthesis (Stata v16.0) is explicitly reported.

elements.quote: Because of the heterogeneity of the studies on patients from different countries, we used the narrative analysis to summarize the outstanding findings of the studies included in the systematic review, and presented the results with tables.
elements.reason: When meta-analysis was not appropriate due to heterogeneity, the authors described using narrative synthesis and presented results in tables.

elements.quote: The results show that the COVID-19 patients with different infection degrees and stages were experiencing different degrees of anxiety, depression, PTSD, insomnia, somatization and fear. The prevalence of anxiety and depression in severe patients was significantly higher than that of other types of patients. The prevalence of anxiety and depression in patients with suspected infection was also higher than other types of patients, possibly because the time of investigation was mainly in the early stage of medical quarantine. The ambiguous diagnosis results may cause anxiety and depression (Chen et al., 2020; Paz et al., 2020; Wesemann et al., 2020). The prevalence of depression and anxiety in patients with mild or stable clinical conditions was significantly lower than that of other patients (Bo et al., 2020; Guo et al., 2020; Ma et al., 2020), which suggested that the effective control of clinical symptoms was closely related to the psychological problems of patients.
elements.reason: The discussion explicitly interprets the review's findings and cites multiple external studies (e.g., Chen et al., Paz et al., Wesemann et al., Bo et al., Guo et al., Ma et al.) to contextualize and explain the observed prevalence differences, satisfying interpretation in the context of other evidence.

elements.quote: According to the investigation time included in the study, the studies included were conducted within half a year after the outbreak of COVID19, especially before March 2020. As this paper is the first known living systematic review, the updated version will be released as more bibliographic search results appear. Deeper analysis on the medical re­ cords (physical or mental diseases) of the SARS-CoV-2 patients will be made to explore the profound impacts of SARS-CoV-2 on patients with chronic disease or those who have suffered from previous trauma in long term. According to the severity of patients, different psychological scales were used to evaluate. For patients with a mild infection, online infor­ mation collection tools could be used (Bo et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2020). For severe patients, face-to-face interviews were used when their condition was stable(Miao et al., 2020; Wu and Peng, 2020). However, due to the lack of research into severe patients, the study on psycho­ logical problems of severe patients may have some deficiencies. Although the review has adopted more strict inclusion and exclusion criteria, the original studies included have found significant heteroge­ neity because of the characteristics of observational studies in epidemic situations. The source of heterogeneity was related to the following reasons: the small sample sizes of some studies were small, non-random sampling method, and different survey scales. This research only included one longitudinal study. It was found that the psychological state changes of COVID-19 patients needed long-term follow-up obser­ vation. If possible, more longitudinal studies should be carried out in the future.
elements.reason: The 'Limitations' section (text_23) explicitly describes several limitations of the included evidence—timing of studies, limited severe-patient data, heterogeneity due to small samples, non-random sampling and varied scales, and scarcity of longitudinal studies—thus discussing limitations of the evidence included.
